title: Should he teach?
hook: he hesitates; Brahma Sahampati asks him to teach; he sees people like lotuses near the surface (MN 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two merchants: Tapussa and Bhallika, their honey-cakes, and the first lay followers.

Have you ever understood something so deeply that you didn't know how to say it? Maybe you went through something hard, a loss, an illness, a recovery, and came out the other side knowing something. Then someone asked you about it, you opened your mouth, and it sounded like a greeting card. Some things don't fit into words very well. The Buddha has found what he was looking for. Now comes a question that's easy to skip past: should he tell anyone at all?
screen: `TOO DEEP FOR WORDS.` → `IT SOUNDED LIKE A GREETING CARD.` → `SHOULD HE TELL ANYONE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this himself. What I've found, he thinks, is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, subtle, beyond mere reasoning. And people love their attachments; they delight in them. For people like that, this would be hard to see. If I taught it, and others didn't understand, that would only be wearying for me. So his mind leans toward not teaching. Then, the sutta says, a great god, Brahma Sahampati, realizes what's happening. The world will be lost, he thinks, if the awakened one stays silent. In the time it takes a strong man to stretch out his bent arm, the god leaves his heaven and appears before the Buddha. He kneels, raises his joined hands, and pleads. Let the Blessed One teach. There are beings with only a little dust in their eyes, losing out because they haven't heard. Some will understand. So the Buddha looks out over the world with the eye of an awakened one, and what he sees is a lotus pond. Some lotuses are still deep under the water. Some have grown right up to the surface. And some stand clear above it, untouched by the water. People are like that: some with much dust in their eyes, some with little, some ready right now. And he decides. Open are the doors to the deathless, he says, for those who have ears. Not everyone is ready. But some are, and for them, it's worth it.
screen: `DEEP, SUBTLE, HARD TO SEE.` · `BRAHMA KNEELS AND PLEADS.` · `A LITTLE DUST IN THEIR EYES.` · `LOTUSES AT EVERY DEPTH.` · then, large: `SOME ARE READY.`

segments.voice: Picture a still pond, green stems reaching up from the mud, and pick one lotus bud to watch as it rises slowly through the dark water toward the light. It breaks the surface, stands in the air with drops of water rolling off, and opens, petal by petal, at its own speed. If your mind wanders, return to the pond.
Paduma. The lotuses in the Buddha's vision of the pond: some still under water, some risen, like people with more or less dust in their eyes.
Your line: some are ready. The doors to the deathless are open. Fifty-nine days in.

screen: `DAY 59 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MAN ON THE ROAD.`

howItsDone: In the Pali telling, Brahma Sahampati's request is the turning point that sets the teaching in motion, and in some traditions a formal request to teach is made to a teacher before a dharma talk, echoing this moment.

fork.setup: you've found something deep and hard to put into words. a god kneels before you: some will understand. what do you do?
options: stay silent: they won't get it.
look out over the world, and decide to teach.
fork.reveal: he surveys the world and sees people like lotuses at every depth. the doors to the deathless are open, he says, and he decides to teach.

original.note: Pali: lotus (Sanskrit padma), one of the flowers in the Buddha's vision of the pond.

trapdoor: what you thought: of course the Buddha wanted to teach.
what it means: he hesitated, because it was so hard to say. a god's plea and a vision of lotuses changed his mind.

what a scholar hears: MN 26 and SN 6.1 (Brahmayacana Sutta): the Buddha's hesitation, Sahampati's request, the blue, red and white lotuses (uppala, paduma, pundarika), and 'open are the doors to the deathless'.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the hesitation and the request
